flashcards.front: What is the primary threat vector for Endpoint Threat Auditing?
flashcards.back_definition: Adversaries exploit local file log deletions on system audit logs to bypass standard perimeter security controls.
flashcards.back_example: Example: Event ID 4625: Logon Failure | Source: 198.51.100.12
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse this threat with other layers (like physical breaches or certificate revocations) which target different assets.
flashcards.back_hook: Recall: local file log deletions is the unlocked door; system audit logs is what the attacker wants to steal.

flashcards.front: How does the security team mitigate Endpoint Threat Auditing threats?
flashcards.back_definition: Deploying and enforcing centralized secure Syslog servers directly hardens system audit logs and blocks unauthorized connections.
flashcards.back_example: Action: Update security configurations to require centralized secure Syslog servers.
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse mitigation (actively blocking the exploit) with detection (simply logging or alerting the event).
flashcards.back_hook: Mitigation is the shield; detection is the security camera.

flashcards.front: How do analysts detect exploitation of Endpoint Threat Auditing?
flashcards.back_definition: By auditing event data and implementing logic flags built to alert on Windows Event ID 4625 flags.
flashcards.back_example: Syslog trace: Event ID 4625: Logon Failure | Source: 198.51.100.12
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse signature-based detection (matching known strings) with anomaly-based detection (mapping dynamic standard deviations).
flashcards.back_hook: Detection is looking for the fingerprint left behind by the threat.
